name: Applications

papers.title: Refinements to precision-information imputation in meta-analysis of survival rates: Boundary correction and cross-study borrowing
papers.abstract: Meta-analyses of survival rates require precision information, such as standard errors (SEs), which is often unreported. We previously proposed imputing missing SEs from reported survival rates, sample sizes, and risk-set sizes. The original method has two limitations. First, it replaces Kaplan--Meier estimates of 1 with 0.99 regardless of sample size. Second, when the risk-set size is unavailable, it uses the total event count as a fallback. The count is often unreported, and the fallback can also substantially overestimate SEs. We propose a sample-size-dependent boundary correction based on a pseudo-event and a method that borrows time-specific event information from studies with available risk-set sizes. In simulations, the boundary correction was more stable than fixed replacement, and borrowing reduced study-level SE imputation bias. Borrowing generally improved precision by retaining studies with missing SEs that lacked both risk-set sizes and event counts.

papers.title: Cutting Bus Service Without Cutting Access: Persistent Homology of Service Deserts and Timetable Reductions
papers.abstract: Japanese bus operators are withdrawing service for lack of drivers, and the choice of which trips to withdraw determines who keeps a bus. We measure service at each stop from vehicle GPS and smart-card records, without timetables, and use persistent homology of walking and walking-plus-waiting time to find enclosed service deserts: pockets surrounded by service but beyond walking distance from it. Around Tsukuba, 35 such pockets lie more than 800m from any station or hourly stop. The 17 that are fully ringed by walkable service hold 18,446 residents. We compare two 2020 timetable reductions by Kanto Railway with random reductions and a heuristic frontier of same-size, capacity-feasible alternatives. At two and four buses an hour, both reductions protected service better than random reductions. No alternative found by the sweep dominates the state-of-emergency timetable. The summer timetable is dominated: it withdrew hourly service from 5,253 residents around stops with almost no morning riders, whereas same-size alternatives kept it for all of them at equal waiting. Averages hide a tail: under the actual timetables, 5.9% and 3.9% of residents are at stops whose expected wait rises by 10 minutes or more, against 0.5% and 0.3% in the alternatives, and capping the increase at 10 minutes at every served stop is feasible at the operator's sizes. If half the removed hours become paid hours saved, the labor saving of both reductions and their main alternatives fall short of the fare revenue on the removed trips.

papers.title: Shooting for Fit: Risk-Averse Stochastic Roster Construction from Bayesian Shot-Pattern Models
papers.abstract: Roster construction is a critical decision problem in professional basketball, requiring teams to balance player quality, player complementarity, and financial constraints under uncertainty. Existing roster optimization models primarily rely on individual player ratings and aggregate performance statistics, which provide limited information about how players' offensive contributions vary with their teammates. Recent advances in player-tracking technology have enabled statistical analyses of spatial shooting patterns, but these insights have rarely informed roster construction. We bridge this gap by developing a data-driven, risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization framework for NBA roster construction. We first develop a Bayesian modeling framework that combines player statistics and spatial shot-chart data to identify player roles and estimate how teammate composition influences shot selection, shooting frequency, and scoring efficiency. The resulting model provides uncertainty-quantified offensive values for hypothetical five-player lineups, including combinations that have never played together. We then formulate roster construction as a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program that optimizes player acquisitions under NBA salary-cap regulations while allowing lineup playing-time allocations to adapt to uncertain player roles. We evaluate the framework using 240 team-offseason decisions over eight seasons and two additional held-out seasons. The results demonstrate that incorporating spatial shooting compatibility substantially changes optimal roster decisions and improves predicted offensive performance relative to approaches based on individual player values. We further find that flexibility in allocating playing time across lineups absorbs much of the uncertainty about player roles.

papers.title: The Illusion of an Automated German Census: Assessing the Feasibility of the 2031 Register-Based Census via Simulation
papers.abstract: The next German Census (2031) is planned to be the country's first fully register-based census, relying exclusively on administrative data sources. In addition to the population registers, ten further administrative registers are envisaged, covering a wide range of information, from driving licences to agricultural social insurance. This study simulates potential data-quality challenges in linking these registers using quasi-identifiers (QIDs), such as names and dates of birth. Using a synthetic population dataset (N=80,206,770), we systematically vary experimental factors related to register characteristics. Across the 1,458 experimental conditions studied, results vary considerably. Some plausible scenarios range from 500,000 to 1,000,000 false-negative linkage errors per linked register. These findings suggest that implementing an automated register-based census using the currently envisaged registers may prove challenging and could require substantial manual post-processing to achieve acceptable data quality.

papers.title: A new method of Ecological Inference based on the Cressie--Read power divergence
papers.abstract: Ecological inference aims to estimate the bivariate association structure between a pair of variables from the row and column totals of a set of contingency tables. The paper introduces a new approach based on minimizing the Cressie--Read power divergence, applied to the estimation of vote transitions between two elections. It also outlines a Fisher scoring algorithm and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimator.

papers.title: Who Fills the Gap? Role Similarity and Teammates' Minutes When NBA Players Are Ruled Out
papers.abstract: When a core player is ruled out before an NBA game, do teammates whose statistical role resembles that of the removed set (every rotation player ruled out, about three per case) play more? Using injury reports stamped at least six hours before tip-off and rosters reconstructed after the season, we study 2,441 team-games from 2023-24 to 2025-26 in which a core player was ruled out for a medical reason. Among teammates in the same game, one within-case standard deviation more similarity in role profile (three-point attempts, assists and rebounds per minute) goes with about 0.63 more minutes, holding reference minutes and headroom fixed (p < 0.0001); this compares teammates within a game, not the minutes gained because of the absence. The pattern holds in two earlier seasons and in exploratory within-player and without-and-with comparisons. Whether similarity adds to listed position is not settled. The association is small and yielded no statistically detectable reduction in the error of the retrospective minute forecasts we tested. Role coverage, how much of the missing minutes and roles the remaining rotation could restore, showed no consistent incremental association with team role output or the final margin.

papers.title: ENSO-linked redistribution of post-monsoon tropical cyclone energy between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal: 1982--2025
papers.abstract: Tropical cyclones in the North Indian Ocean (NIO) form in two sub-basins, the Arabian Sea (AS) and the Bay of Bengal (BoB), which are usually studied separately, with their relationship to the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) treated as stationary. We develop a joint inter-basin statistical framework and apply it to 416 disturbances from quality-controlled IBTrACS best tracks for 1982--2025, with harmonised IMD and JTWC intensities, ERA5 and ERSSTv5. The framework tests whether ENSO changes the basin total or redistributes energy between the sub-basins, separates its effect on formation from that on intensification, attributes each sub-basin's response to environmental terms along individual tracks, and tests stationarity and the record length needed to detect trends. In October-December, ENSO redistributes rather than changes the total: for a one-standard-deviation increase in Ni\~no-3.4 (about 1 $^\circ$C), accumulated cyclone energy (ACE) is multiplied by 1.89 in the AS and by 0.63 in the BoB, while the NIO total shows no detectable change (factor 0.99 [0.74, 1.32]). ENSO acts on intensification, with no detectable effect on formation: the odds that a cyclonic storm becomes very severe rise about fourfold in the AS and halve in the BoB, through lower vertical wind shear (VWS) over the AS and weaker low-level vorticity over the BoB. The relationship has changed: El Ni\~no lowered total NIO energy in 1982--2003, but in 2004-2025 AS gains balanced BoB losses (change p = 0.016). Very severe storms and rapid intensification increased in the AS only, and no 15-year window detects this increase, so about three decades of data are needed. The post-monsoon IOD signal can hardly be separated from ENSO, and August Ni\~no-3.4 gives modest skill for the AS-BoB partition but none for the basin total.

papers.title: Atheism and Cross-Country National Cognitive Skills: Evidence from a Beta Regression Analysis
papers.abstract: This study performs a beta regression analysis to investigate how country-level cognitive skills---measured using harmonized large-scale international educational assessments and expressed on an IQ-type scale---are associated with the prevalence of atheism in 131 countries. We find that this association is nonlinear: at low levels of cognitive skills, increases are associated with lower expected levels of atheism, whereas beyond a threshold, they are associated with higher expected atheism rates. This turning point is estimated to occur at approximately 65 on the IQ-type scale. The strength and location of the relationship vary across regions. We estimate elasticities of expected atheism rates with respect to cognitive skills for all countries in the sample and introduce the concept of the atheism gap to identify countries where observed prevalence is substantially higher or lower than predicted by their conditioning variables.

papers.title: When precision exceeds fidelity: systematic error quantification for inference with misspecified simulators
papers.abstract: As scientific datasets grow in complexity and precision, the primary source of uncertainty in parameter inference shifts from measurement noise to systematic errors within the simulators themselves. In this setting, Bayesian evidence concentrates on whichever misspecified model best approximates the data. Evidence-weighted model averaging can then underestimate systematic uncertainty when one model component compensates for the misspecification of another component. We posit that in this case, the key question is how each model responds to discrepancies between simulator and data. We show that the local response of an inferred parameter to perturbations in the data --- the model's influence map --- can be estimated efficiently from forward evaluations of the simulator at existing posterior samples. Propagating discrepancy residuals through these influence maps enables individual sources of systematic bias to be isolated. Applied to independent observations used to infer the mass of a supermassive black hole, we find that the error is dominated by model systematics. We identify a simplification shared by all models, propagate the discrepancies through each model's influence map, and apply a first-order correction of the resulting biases. This substantially improves the cross-observation consistency of the inferred black-hole mass within each model while preserving the between-model spread that represents remaining systematics.

papers.title: A Quantile-Based Framework for Bimodal Distribution Construction
papers.abstract: This study suggests a novel quantile-based framework to construct bimodal distribution which does not rely on mixture representations or closed-form probability density functions. This proposed approach induces bimodality by transforming the quantile density through a strictly positive modulation function so that it can preserve the support and tail behavior of a chosen baseline distribution with providing explicit control over modal structure. The method is shown to apply broadly across bounded, semi-bounded and unbounded distribution families which include power, reflected power, logistic, Weibull and generalized lambda distributions. Simulation studies and a real-data application were performed which have shown that the proposed construction yields smooth, interpretable and computationally stable bimodal models and it also provides a flexible alternative to classical mixture-based approaches. Also this framework allows gradual transitions between unimodal and bimodal shapes which make it well suited for modeling overlapping regimes which are commonly encountered in real-world data. This proposed methodology therefor offers a robust and interpretable tool for bimodal modeling without requiring latent class assumptions or complex estimation procedures.

papers.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
papers.abstract: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.

papers.title: Simple, general strategies for correcting the upward bias of calibration summaries of prediction models
papers.abstract: For clinical prediction models, calibration across the spectrum of predicted values is often assessed via flexible calibration curves and associated scalar summaries such as the integrated calibration index (ICI). However, these scalar summaries tend to have a finite-sample upward bias, as they are based on the absolute value of an estimate whose sampling distribution can cross zero. We show the mechanism underlying this bias and quantify its magnitude as a function of the true calibration error and its variance. This mechanism motivates easily implementable methods for reducing the bias (plug-in and inversion methods, each applied locally or globally) that are applicable to any smoothing method that generates an estimate and its sampling variance for each point on the calibration curve. These methods are general in that 1) they can be used for different outcome types (continuous, binary, time-to-event, as well as counterfactual outcomes for models that predict treatment benefit), and 2) the resulting bias-adjusted calibration error curves yield bias-corrected estimates of other metrics such as quantile-based ones (e.g., E50 and E90). Focusing on ICI as an exemplary metric, numerical and case studies demonstrate that the upward bias can be substantial, especially when the sample is small and the true ICI is close to zero. Results show that the Global Inversion method removed the most bias, particularly when the bias was substantial, although it could slightly increase the mean absolute error if the bias was small.

papers.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis
papers.abstract: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

papers.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many complex networks involve time-varying relations between more than two nodes. Such networks are naturally modeled by temporal hypergraphs. We propose the Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model (HHCM), a semi-mechanistic model for temporal hypergraphs that combines a Hawkes process to model the timestamps of hyperedges with a noisy copy mechanism to model the nodes present in hyperedges. Each hyperedge is either generated as an exogenous event with a baseline rate or an endogenous event as a noisy copy of a previous hyperedge. Our proposed model can be used for credit attribution, where the objective is to quantify the influence or contribution of a prior hyperedge to a current one. We apply the HHCM to perform attribution on several real network datasets with higher-order relations, including email networks and militarized interstate dispute networks.

papers.title: Modeling time series of high-resolution spectra using the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition with application to radial velocity exoplanet searches
papers.abstract: We describe a framework for building low-rank separable expansions to model spectroscopic data from systems with time-varying spectra, in settings where the spectral dimension is finely sampled (in wavelength), but the temporal dimension is sparsely and possibly irregulary sampled. The motivating application is detection and characterization of small exoplanets, e.g., Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars. Such planets cannot be seen directly, but can be detected via the minute Doppler shifts of the host star spectrum due to the star's motion as the planet and star revolve around their mutual center of mass. Current instruments are reaching the precision necessary to detect the ~10 cm/s motions corresponding to an exo-Earth. But the small Doppler shifts from such low-amplitude orbital motion can be masked or mimicked by the effects of stellar activity on the surface of the host star. e.g., starspots (dark regions), faculae (bright filaments), etc. One technique astronomers have used to try to model the stellar activity component of the signal is PCA, applied to an ensemble of spectra collected over time. But PCA neglects the continuous function nature of a spectrum at a given time, and the continuous evolution of spectra over time. We address model building from a function approximation perspective, via the asymmetric Hilbert-Schmidt decomposition (HSD). This provides a PCA-like low-rank decomposition of a dynamic spectrum, but it explicitly accounts for time dependence, both estimating temporal basis functions, and accounting for irregular temporal sampling when estimating spectral basis functions. We show that HSD improves the fidelity of a fixed-order model of the dynamic spectrum of a Sun-like star with a starspot, with mean squared error for spectral basis functions many times smaller than achieved via PCA when spectra are randomly sampled sparsely and irregularly in time.

papers.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
papers.abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.
